section.title: Least action and the shape of a path

introduction.p: Some optimization problems vary an entire path rather than a single number. A path determines an integral, called a functional, and small changes in the path change that integral. We will use differentiation and integration by parts to find a condition for a stationary value. Stationary does not necessarily mean minimal.

exercise.title: Why is optimizing a path different from optimizing a number?

statement.p: Ordinary optimization chooses a number that makes a function extreme. A path problem chooses a whole function. In your own words, why is arc length a functional rather than an ordinary function, and why does testing a path require wiggling it?

hint.p: The input is now a curve, and the output is one number such as length or time. A nearby competitor is the original path plus a small wiggle that keeps the endpoints fixed.

subsection.title: The brachistochrone problem
subsection.p: One of the most famous path problems asks for the fastest slide.
Place a bead at a point A. Let it slide without friction under gravity to a lower point B. We may choose the shape of the wire connecting A to B.
Which wire gives the shortest travel time?
The shortest path is a straight line. But the fastest path is not a straight line. A path that drops steeply at first lets the bead gain speed quickly, and that speed can help later.
This is the brachistochrone problem. The word comes from Greek roots meaning “shortest time.”

note.title: Lesson of the brachistochrone
note.p: The best path depends on what is being optimized.
Shortest distance and shortest time are different questions.

subsection.p: The full proof that the cycloid is the fastest curve belongs to the calculus of variations. But the setup already shows the new kind of calculus: an integral depends on a path, and we seek the path that makes the integral extreme.

exercise.title: Why is the fastest path not the shortest path?

statement.p: The brachistochrone is a cycloid, not a straight line. In your own words, why can dropping steeply at first produce a shorter travel time even though the path is longer, and what does that say about the quantity being optimized?

hint.p: Time is distance over speed, and speed is gained by falling. A path that gathers speed early can win on time while losing on length. The best path depends on what the integral is measuring.

exercise.title: Why is a first variation the analogue of a derivative being zero?

statement.p: If a path is shortest, every allowed wiggle should give a critical value at wiggle size zero. In your own words, why does \mathcal{L}'(0)=0 for every endpoint-fixing wiggle play the role of f'(c)=0, and why do the boundary terms from integration by parts disappear?

hint.p: The unknown is the whole path, so the test must work against every small deformation. Fixed endpoints force the wiggle to vanish at the ends, which kills the boundary term and leaves an interior condition on the path.

note.title: Stationary does not always mean minimum
note.p: The historical phrase is “least action,” but the safest calculus statement is
This is like ordinary calculus: f'(c)=0 may indicate a minimum, a maximum, or neither. More work is needed to decide which.

paragraphs.p: This is why the subject goes beyond the ordinary single-variable course. We need to make sense of spaces of functions, allowed variations, endpoint conditions, existence of minimizers, and the difference between minimum and stationary.
But the seed is already here:

p.em: differentiate an accumulated quantity, watch the boundary terms, and set the first variation to zero.

paragraphs.p: That sentence connects much of the road ahead. In multivariable calculus, the boundary of an interval becomes the boundary of a region. Flux through endpoints becomes flux through curves and surfaces. The Fundamental Theorem becomes Green’s theorem, the Divergence Theorem, and Stokes’ theorem.
The book began with distance and velocity. It ends by pointing to the same pattern in larger geometry:

p.me: \text{change inside is measured by derivatives and boundaries.}

exercise.title: Why does least action live beyond single-variable calculus?

statement.p: The Euler–Lagrange equation is a stationarity condition for a functional whose input is a path. Explain how integrating kinetic minus potential energy defines the action and why this optimization differs from varying a single real number.

hint.p: You are no longer choosing one number; you are choosing a motion x(t). Stationary action is the condition that this motion not change the integral to first order under wiggles, which recovers the laws of mechanics as a variational statement.
